results.content: However, even after training a high-performing logistic regression model, the process of setting appropriate decision thresholds and calibrating probability outputs can be challenging. By the end, you'll have a solid understanding of how to optimize your logistic regression models for improved decision-making and reliable probability estimates. In logistic regression, the model outputs a probability value between 0 and 1 for each data instance, representing the likelihood of the instance belonging to the positive class. Even after selecting an appropriate decision threshold, the probabilities output by a logistic regression model may not accurately reflect the true underlying probabilities. Two popular techniques for calibrating logistic regression probabilities are Platt scaling and isotonic regression. Platt scaling [1] is a post-processing method that fits a sigmoid function to the model's output probabilities to map them to better-calibrated probabilities. Isotonic regression [2] is a non-parametric technique that learns a monotonically increasing function to map the model's output probabilities to better-calibrated probabilities. * Use the isotonic regression algorithm to learn the calibration function from the validation set probabilities. 1. **Threshold Optimization**: For both the uncalibrated and calibrated models, optimize the decision threshold to maximize a chosen performance metric (e.g., F1-score) on the validation set. flowchart TD A["Data Preparation"] --> B["Train Logistic Regression"] B --> C["Evaluate Uncalibrated Performance"] C --> D["Platt Scaling Calibration"] C --> E["Isotonic Regression Calibration"] D --> F["Threshold Optimization"] E --> F F --> G["Evaluate on Test Set"]. By understanding the impact of decision thresholds and the benefits of calibration techniques like Platt scaling and isotonic regression, you can significantly improve the predictive reliability and real-world applicability of your logistic regression models. results.title: An introduction to calibration (part II): Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and beta calibration.
results.content: # An introduction to calibration (part II): Platt scaling, isotonic regression, and beta calibration. ## Calibrators are tools used to transform the scores generated by your models into (almost) real mathematical probabilities. Some of the calibration maps that can be obtained through Platt scaling. As discussed in *Beyond sigmoids*2, this method can lead to quite good calibrations as long as the ratio of the score distributions for both binary classes is similar to the ratio of two Gaussian distributions with equal variance. Unfortunately, if this is not the case, Platt scaling can actually lead to even worse calibrated scores, as the identity function is not present in the family of functions that can be obtained from (1), which means it would leave the scores untouched if there is no better calibration. *Isotonic regression*3 is a calibration method that provides a discrete, step-wise, monotonically increasing calibration map consisting of a set of points arranged in a staircase-like way. The calibration map for isotonic regression is obtained by minimising. Thanks to not assuming anything about the score distribution, a calibration of this kind should be able to correct any monotonic distortion coming from an uncalibrated model. However, it also has two major disadvantages: it cannot provide good calibrations when non-monotonic corrections are needed (this is shared with Platt scaling), and it usually requires a vast amount of data compared to parametrics methods as it is prone to overfitting. First of all, beta calibration is a parametric method, so having a small data set is not as problematic as for isotonic regression. Thus, beta calibration not only provides a wider set of maps, but it also guarantees up to some point that it will not worsen the calibration of the original model if it is already calibrated or if no optimal calibration maps are found. Although this is usually a good idea to avoid overfitting to the training set, if the original model is ill-calibrated with non-monotonic distortions, beta calibration will not be capable of obtaining well-calibrated scores.
